h1:
Thai-Lao Friendship Bridge
A Day Trip Across to Vientiane
intro: The Thai-Lao Friendship Bridge No. 1 spans the Mekong River and links Nong Khai with the Lao side, and it makes hopping over to Vientiane easier than most people expect. With a Thai passport you don't need a visa in advance — you just board the cross-border bus and ride straight across. Plenty of travelers use Nong Khai as their base and pop over to Vientiane for the day: browse the morning market, pay respects at That Luang, snap a photo at Patuxai, grab lunch, then head back to sleep on the Thai side. This guide walks you through the crossing step by step — what documents to bring, how much it costs, what time the checkpoint opens, and how to plan a one-day timeline so you don't miss the last bus back. We'll also tell you straight where people tend to get stuck and where you can save time.

blocks.html: The Thai-Lao Friendship Bridge No. 1 has been open since 1994 and was the first bridge across the Mekong between the two countries. The Thai end sits in Muang Nong Khai district, about 2 km from the town center, while the Lao end is at Ban Tha Na Laeng, roughly 20 km from central Vientiane. Pedestrians and motorbikes aren't allowed to cross the bridge itself — you have to take the cross-border bus, a car, or one of the shuttle vehicles — because a railway line runs down the middle of the span as well. The route most Thai travelers use is the cross-border bus that runs straight from Nong Khai bus terminal to the Vientiane bus station, clearing immigration on both sides in a single trip.

blocks.text: What documents do you need to cross?

blocks.html: What you need depends on how far you plan to go. Thai nationals have two options: if you're only heading to Vientiane and nearby towns, a temporary border pass is enough. But if you want to travel deeper into Laos — Vang Vieng, Luang Prabang and so on — you'll need a passport.

items: Thai passport — the easiest route. No visa needed in advance, you can enter Laos and continue on to other towns, and officers stamp you at the checkpoint on both sides. Most Thai travelers go this way because it's simple and leaves your options open.

Temporary border pass — for those without a passport. You can get one at the Nong Khai provincial hall (district administration office) using your Thai ID card and a photo, for a small fee. It only covers Vientiane Capital and is valid for a set window of time — you can't go any further than that.
Children and dependents — kids need their own documents. Have a copy of the birth certificate or the child's passport ready.
Cash — bring Thai baht and Lao kip, or use baht at tourist-facing shops on the Vientiane side. Currency exchange booths are available at the checkpoint and in town.

blocks.title: Straight talk on documents
blocks.html: If you don't have a passport yet and only plan to cross to Vientiane now and then, the border pass is cheaper and easy to arrange. But if you think you might want to travel further into Laos down the line, just get a passport — it's the cleaner option, since the border pass only covers the Vientiane area. Rules and fees on the Lao side change from time to time, so check with the Nong Khai customs checkpoint before you go to be sure.

blocks.text: The border crossing, step by step

blocks.html: If you don't have a car, the easiest way is the international cross-border bus from Nong Khai bus terminal. The bus takes you through both checkpoints itself — no need to find onward transport along the way. Here's how it actually goes.

items.activity: Buy the cross-border bus ticket at Nong Khai bus terminal
items.note: Tell the staff you're heading to Vientiane, take your ticket, and board on the next departure.

items.activity: Stop at Thai immigration for exit formalities
items.note: The bus pulls up at the Thai checkpoint; hand over your passport or border pass for the exit stamp, then reboard the same bus.

items.activity: The bus crosses the Friendship Bridge over the Mekong
items.note: It's a short span with river views on both sides — you can take photos from the bus.

items.activity: Stop at Lao immigration for entry formalities and the fee
items.note: Fill out the entry form, get your entry stamp, and pay a small fee on the Lao side (more expensive on holidays than weekdays).

items.activity: Reboard and ride to Vientiane bus station (Morning Market)
items.note: The terminus is in the city center — walk on from there or grab a tuk-tuk to the sights.

blocks.title: Keep your ticket and documents close
blocks.html: When you get off for immigration, the bus waits at the checkpoint — don't leave your belongings on board if you're not sure, and keep your ticket and crossing documents on you the whole time, since officers may ask to see them again on the way back. On the morning of a long weekend the crowds swell and immigration lines can be long, so give yourself a little buffer.

The international cross-border bus, route 1, runs straight from Nong Khai bus terminal to the Vientiane bus station (near the Morning Market), a distance of about 27 km, with the whole trip including immigration taking around 2 hours. It's the option most people without a car rely on, because the bus handles both checkpoints in a single trip.

items: Fare — around 55 THB on weekdays and around 60 THB on weekends and public holidays (not including the Lao immigration fee).

Approximate schedule — several departures a day; the morning runs start around 07:30 and continue through the day into the evening, with the last departure around 18:00 (schedules change, so check at the terminal before you travel).
Where to board — Nong Khai bus terminal; buy your ticket at the cross-border bus counter inside the station.
Lao-side terminus — Vientiane bus station by the Morning Market, right in the city center, so you can start sightseeing on foot.

blocks.title: Want more flexibility? Try another way
blocks.html: If you'd rather not wait for the bus schedule, another option is to take one of the bridge shuttle vehicles across to the Lao side and then arrange a tuk-tuk or onward transport into town yourself. It's more flexible on timing, but you'll change vehicles several times and have to haggle on the fare. If you drive your own car, you can cross, but you'll need extra paperwork and Lao-side insurance for the vehicle, which is more hassle for a single day. For a day trip, the cross-border bus is the most straightforward.

blocks.text: On a day trip, what can you see in Vientiane?

blocks.html: Vientiane is an easy capital to explore on foot — the main sights cluster fairly close together, so you can cover the headline landmarks in a single day. These are the spots day-trippers tend to stop at.

items.name: Pha That Luang (That Luang)
items.blurb: The golden stupa that symbolizes Laos and the most sacred site the Lao people take pride in. It photographs beautifully when the sun catches the gold, and there's a small entry fee.

items.name: Patuxai
items.blurb: An arch in the city center reminiscent of the Arc de Triomphe; climb to the top for views over Vientiane. It's ringed by a fountain park that's pleasant for a stroll and photos.

items.name: Wat Si Muang / Haw Phra Kaew
items.blurb: An old temple in the city center where locals come to make wishes, near Haw Phra Kaew, which once housed the Emerald Buddha — close enough to walk between the two.

items.name: Vientiane Morning Market
items.blurb: A big central market with food, Lao woven textiles, silverware and souvenirs, right next to the bus station — easy to swing by before you board for home.

items.name: Vientiane Mekong riverfront
items.blurb: The Lao-side riverside walk has an evening market and restaurants, and you can look back across to the Thai side. A nice spot for a lunch in the breeze.

blocks.title: Where people get stuck vs. what you can skip
blocks.html: That Luang and Patuxai give you the most for a single day — both photograph well and sit close together. The Morning Market is right by the bus station, so you can browse it while waiting for the bus back. If time is tight, don't force yourself to hit every temple; pick 2-3 main spots and leave room for a relaxed lunch by the Mekong rather than rushing yourself into the ground.

blocks.text: A one-day timeline that catches the bus back

blocks.html: The key to a day trip is leaving enough time to catch one of the return buses. Where a lot of people slip up is losing track of time and missing the evening departure, then having to arrange their own crossing after dark, which is far more of a hassle. Plan it like this and you'll be relaxed and on time.

items.activity: Board the morning cross-border bus at Nong Khai bus terminal
items.note: Going early gives you a full day of sightseeing, and the morning immigration lines aren't long yet.

items.activity: Arrive at Vientiane bus station (Morning Market)
items.note: Grab a tuk-tuk or hire a car — always agree on the price before you get in.
Knock out the two main landmarks in the morning while the sun isn't too harsh — great for photos.

items.activity: Lunch by the Mekong or in town
items.note: Try Lao dishes — khao piak sen, pho, Lao-style som tam — sitting in the river breeze.

items.activity: Walk Wat Si Muang / Haw Phra Kaew, then shop the Morning Market
items.note: Pick up Lao woven textiles, silverware and souvenirs before heading back.

items.activity: Return to the bus station and wait for the return bus
items.note: Leave time for immigration on both sides on the way back — don't cut it too close to the last departure.

items.activity: Arrive in Nong Khai and head back to your Thai-side accommodation
items.note: Round off the evening along the Nong Khai riverfront or the walking street at an easy pace.

blocks.title: Don't bank on the very last departure
blocks.html: On the way back you'll clear immigration on both sides again, so if you aim for the very last bus and the line is long or you miss it, you'll be stuck arranging a crossing after dark. Better to target a departure with one more in reserve — it's a lot more reassuring. And always keep some Thai baht on you for fees or onward transport.

items: Cross-border bus fare — around 55 THB on weekdays / around 60 THB on holidays, per trip.
Lao-side crossing fee — a small fee applies at Lao immigration, usually higher on weekends and holidays than on weekdays. Have cash in baht or kip ready.

Checkpoint hours — the Friendship Bridge checkpoint is open for crossings from morning to night every day, generally around 06:00 to around 22:00, but the cross-border bus only runs until the evening, so plan around the bus schedule.
Keep a cash reserve — exchange booths are available at the checkpoint and around Vientiane, but rates in town are usually better. Bring baht to exchange, or spend it directly at tourist-facing shops.

blocks.html: Fees and schedules change from time to time, especially on the Lao side, so before you actually travel, check again with the Nong Khai bus terminal or the customs checkpoint to be sure. A number many people use to ask is the Nong Khai bus office: 042-412-679.

blocks.text: Photographing the bridge from the Nong Khai side

blocks.html: If you're not ready to cross but still want to see the bridge, the Nong Khai side has some lovely photo angles. The popular spots are the Nong Khai riverside walk and the riverfront cafes that look out at the span reaching across the Mekong to the Lao side. Late afternoon, when the sun softens, is the prettiest time — you get the bridge, the Mekong and the sunset all in one frame. If you come to Nong Khai and don't cross the border, just sitting by the river watching the bridge is the image that'll stay with you of this town.

faq.q: Do Thai nationals need a visa to cross the Friendship Bridge to Vientiane?
faq.a: No. Thai nationals can enter Laos on a passport without a visa in advance, with entry and exit stamps at the checkpoint on both sides. If you don't have a passport and are only going to Vientiane, you can use a temporary border pass instead, arranged at the Nong Khai provincial hall.

faq.q: Can you do Vientiane as a day trip?
faq.a: Yes. If you take the morning cross-border bus around 07:30, you'll reach Vientiane around 09:30, with time to take in That Luang, Patuxai and the Morning Market at an easy pace before heading back in the afternoon or evening. The key is not to bank on the very last bus — leave time for immigration on both sides on the way back.

faq.q: How much is the Nong Khai-Vientiane cross-border bus, and where do you board?
faq.a: The fare is around 55 THB on weekdays and around 60 THB on weekends and holidays. You board at Nong Khai bus terminal and buy your ticket at the cross-border bus counter. The bus runs straight to the Vientiane bus station by the Morning Market, with the whole trip including immigration taking about 2 hours.

faq.q: Can you walk across the Thai-Lao Friendship Bridge?
faq.a: No. Pedestrians and motorbikes aren't allowed to cross the bridge, because a railway line runs down the middle of the span. You have to take the cross-border bus, a car, or one of the shuttle vehicles. The easiest option for those without a car is the cross-border bus, which takes you through both checkpoints in a single trip.

faq.q: What time does the Friendship Bridge checkpoint open?
faq.a: The checkpoint is open for crossings from morning to night every day, generally around 06:00 to around 22:00. But the cross-border bus only runs until the evening, around 18:00, so for a day trip, plan around the bus schedule. Both fees and schedules change from time to time, so check with the Nong Khai bus terminal before you travel to be sure.
